source.title: Constructing Ophthalmic MLLM for Positioning-diagnosis Collaboration Through Clinical Cognitive Chain Reasoning

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendix material, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how dataset size relates to downstream accuracy in a fine-tuned ophthalmic multimodal model, an extension to a new modality and training regime rather than the original language-model pretraining-loss measurement.
record.gate_note: The paper reports subset-scaling results for downstream clinical QA accuracy and comparisons between two data sources. The model-comparison and ablation results unrelated to scaling are not rows. It does not report held-out pretraining loss, parameter-count/token/compute scaling, or a compute-optimal allocation.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes InternVL2.5-8B on growing subsets of two ophthalmic instruction datasets and fits a power law to downstream QA accuracy against data percentage (Section 5.2, Fig. 5). That is a data-scaling result in a new modality and fine-tuning regime (V5), measured on downstream tasks (V6). It reports no pretraining loss, no parameter or compute scaling, and no compute-optimal split.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors claim a scaling law between FundusGen data volume and accuracy (stated as L ∝ N^0.068, where the measure is accuracy). They argue that cognitive-aligned annotations raise data utilization efficiency. The abstract frames the law as being between data quality and capability, but the experiment varies volume. The comparison dataset shows no significant improvement with more data.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales fine-tuning data volume for a single 8B ophthalmic multimodal model and measures downstream QA accuracy, rather than scaling language-model pretraining parameters, tokens, or compute and measuring held-out loss.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed scaling behavior differs by data source: FundusGen shows an accuracy trend, while Classification Annotation-Guided Data does not show significant improvement on GMAI-MMBench.
record.problems: The scaling experiment varies data volume for one stated model size and measures downstream accuracy, not pretraining loss. Exact plotted values for most points are not stated in the text; only the GMAI-MMBench FundusGen fit statistics are reported. The comparison-dataset curve on Fundus-MMBench is not described in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant scaling results left out. Other benchmark comparisons, dataset ablations, and pseudo-label experiments were omitted because they do not measure accuracy scaling with data quantity.

Predictability from pretraining loss. Scaling across model sizes. Extrapolation to larger data scales.

Entire version: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
Entire version: no shape or architecture variation at fixed size.

missing.what: Fit statistics for the FundusGen curve on Fundus-MMBench: R²=0.904, adj R²=0.761, MSE=0.0003
Fine-tuning on 10% of FundusGen matches 100% of the comparison data on GMAI-MMBench (a data-efficiency result)

record.verdict_notes: The evidence for scaling is weak in kind. The experiment uses a single 8B model and varies the percentage of fine-tuning data over about one decade, with an unstated number of points. The exponent is fitted to accuracy, and no error bars or seeds are reported, so the record's 'uncertainty_reported: y' looks wrong. Neither original source is involved. The V7 links were removed: the data-source contrast is a scope limit on V5/V6, not evidence that exponents vary with fitting choices.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, training tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs' held-out pretraining loss from smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their growth with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The paper tests scaling with training-data quantity for ophthalmic multimodal fine-tuning, but not the same loss-based law in image/video pretraining, repeated-data training, or transfer regimes.
Downstream QA accuracy is measured against data quantity; the paper does not test predictability from pretraining loss or across a range of model sizes.
The paper compares data sources, but does not test parameter-count/token/compute exponents, compute-optimal splits, fitting-method choices, or whether curves bend at larger scales.

rows.subject: InternVL2.5-8B
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuning on increasing subsets of FundusGen and fitting accuracy against data percentage.
rows.measure: Clinical QA accuracy versus data percentage; fitted power law.
rows.value: L ∝ N^0.068; R² = 0.972, adjusted R² = 0.930, MSE = 0.0001; accuracy shows a stable and predictable upward trend as data volume increases.
rows.note: The paper describes this as a scaling law for GMAI-MMBench accuracy. The reported fit statistics are for this FundusGen curve.
rows.check: The fit is of accuracy, not loss, despite the 'L' notation. The x-axis spans only about one decade (roughly 10% to 100%), and the number of subset points is not stated. For V5 this is a power-law form for accuracy, not the loss law. The V7 link is dropped: a single fitted exponent says nothing about whether exponents depend on fitting choices.

rows.subject: InternVL2.5-8B
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuning on increasing subsets of Classification Annotation-Guided Data and comparing accuracy against data percentage.
rows.measure: Clinical QA accuracy versus data percentage.
rows.value: No significant performance improvement as data size increases; performance declines in some data intervals.
rows.note: The paper also states that fine-tuning on 10% of FundusGen produces results comparable to 100% of this comparison dataset.
rows.check: The comparison data shows no significant gain with more data and declines in some intervals. This bears on whether data scaling holds for every data source (V5/V6). It is not about how exponents or splits depend on fitting choices (V7), so the V7 link is dropped.

relationships.condition: FundusGen fine-tuning data, InternVL2.5-8B, about one decade of data percentage
relationships.reason: Accuracy follows a fitted power law (exponent 0.068, R²=0.972) on GMAI-MMBench. It also follows a weaker fit (adj R²=0.761) on Fundus-MMBench (r1, r3). This is an accuracy-based form, not loss.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy fitted a power law with exponent 0.068 and R² of 0.972 on GMAI-MMBench, while Fundus-MMBench had a weaker adjusted R² of 0.761.

relationships.reason: The same model and regime show no significant gain with more data, and declines in some intervals (r2). Scaling depends on the data source.
relationships.display_finding: Additional data produced no significant performance gain and caused declines over some intervals.

relationships.condition: FundusGen data scaling, clinical QA benchmarks
relationships.reason: Downstream QA accuracy rises steadily with data volume, with a good power-law fit on GMAI-MMBench and a weaker one on Fundus-MMBench (r1, r3).
relationships.display_finding: Clinical QA accuracy increases steadily with data volume, with a good power-law fit on GMAI-MMBench and a weaker fit on Fundus-MMBench.

relationships.reason: Accuracy does not improve predictably with data size, and drops in some intervals (r2).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy declined over some data-size intervals rather than improving predictably.
